title: Rules of Hooks Dynamic Validator
subtopicTitle: Hooks Linked List & Rules of Hooks
concept: Detecting Conditional or Shuffled Hook Calls
problemStatement: Implement `validateHookSequence(mountHooks, updateHooks)` that compares the sequence of hook types called on mount vs update. If update calls fewer hooks, more hooks, or a different hook type at any index, throws an Error detailing the exact violation.
interviewTrap: This is the exact runtime error React throws: 'Rendered fewer hooks than expected. This may be caused by an accidental early return statement.'

testCases.name: Validates identical hook sequences across renders
Throws error when hook count changes between renders
testCases.input: mount 3 hooks, update 2 hooks throws Error
testCases.testFn: try { validateHookSequence(['useState', 'useRef', 'useEffect'], ['useState', 'useEffect']); return false; } catch (e) { return true; }

testCases.name: Throws error when hook type order is transposed

testCases.testFn: try { validateHookSequence(['useState', 'useEffect'], ['useEffect', 'useState']); return false; } catch (e) { return e.message.includes('Hook type mismatch'); }

detailedExplanation.conceptualOverview: The fundamental Rule of Hooks ('Only Call Hooks at the Top Level — do not call inside loops, conditions, or nested functions') exists because React relies exclusively on the sequential call order of hooks to match state. A dynamic validator detects hook count or type mismatches across renders and throws an error.
stepByStepWalkthrough: Maintain record of hooks called during initial mount: `expectedHookSequence = ['state', 'effect', 'state']`.
On subsequent re-renders, track each hook call index and type.
If a conditional statement omits a hook or changes the order (e.g. calling 'effect' when 'state' was expected):
Immediately detect mismatch: `Rendered fewer hooks than expected` or `Hook type mismatch at index i`.
Throw descriptive error matching React's internal invariant violation.
Validator confirms strict obedience to the Rules of Hooks.
detailedExplanation.underlyingEngineInternals: In React's `ReactFiberHooks.js`, if `updateWorkInProgressHook` finds that `nextHook` is null while the component is still executing hooks, React throws: `Error: Rendered more hooks than during the previous render`. If the component finishes with unvisited hooks left over, it throws: `Error: Rendered fewer hooks than during the previous render`.

complexity.time: O(H) validation over H hook calls.

specifications: React Official Docs: Rules of Hooks
verifiedRules: Hooks must be called in the exact same order on every render.
Violating call order corrupts internal linked list pointers and throws invariant errors.

interviewCrossQuestions.question: What specific internal error does React throw when a hook is called conditionally?
interviewCrossQuestions.answer: If a component calls fewer hooks than previous render, React throws: `Error: Rendered fewer hooks than during the previous render`. If it calls more, it throws: `Error: Rendered more hooks than during the previous render`. This occurs because `workInProgressHook` cursor hits `null` prematurely or finds unvisited nodes left on the linked list.
interviewCrossQuestions.whyAsked: Checks if candidate has encountered and understands real React runtime invariant violations.

realWorldUseCases.description: Static AST linters verifying that hooks are only called at the top level of component functions.

howToExplain.opening: The Rule of Hooks exists because React relies exclusively on call order to match hook state to the fiber's linked list across renders.
keyPoints: Skipping a hook misaligns all subsequent hook nodes on the linked list.
Results in state swapping between completely unrelated hooks.
Throws invariant error: Rendered more/fewer hooks than previous render.
Hooks must only be called at the top level, never inside conditions or loops.
howToExplain.closingImpression: The Rules of Hooks are not an arbitrary stylistic guideline; they are an architectural constraint imposed by singly-linked list state storage.
analogies: A combination lock: you must enter the exact sequence of numbers in order; skipping a number jams the lock.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling hooks inside early return branches: `if (!user) return null; const [data] = useState();`
commonMistakes.why: If user is null on render 1 and present on render 2, the hook count changes, throwing an invariant error.
commonMistakes.correct: Move all hook calls above all conditional return statements.

followUpDeepDive.question: How does React detect hook order swaps between different hook types (e.g. useState swapped for useEffect)?
followUpDeepDive.answer: In development mode, React attaches internal tags to hook nodes. If the hook type at index `i` does not match the tag stored during mount, React logs a descriptive warning detailing the exact hook type mismatch.
